entries.question: Walk through the front door of the home you remember best from childhood. What is the first thing you see, hear, and smell?
entries.answer: The green front door, first of all. It stuck every time it rained, so you had to put your shoulder to it and push until it gave. Inside it smelled of rice cooking and floor wax, and a little of the kerosene Papa kept by the lamp for when the power went out. Mama always had the radio on low in the kitchen, so you heard music before you heard anybody talking. Even now the smell of floor wax makes me want to take my shoes off at the door.
entries.page:
The front door of Rosa's childhood home was green, and when it rained it stuck. She put her shoulder to it and pushed until it gave.

Inside, the house smelled of rice cooking and floor wax, and a little of the kerosene Papa kept by the lamp for when the power went out.

Mama had the radio on low in the kitchen. Rosa heard music before she heard anybody talking.

Even now, the smell of floor wax makes her want to take her shoes off at the door.

entries.question: Where in that home did you feel safest? Describe the spot.
entries.answer: Under the stairs, where the brooms were kept. There was a gap at the back just big enough for me, and I kept a biscuit tin there with a blue ribbon tied around it. Inside were two marbles, one cloudy and one clear, and the only photograph I had of my grandmother, in a dress with a white collar. When the house got loud I crawled in with the tin on my knees and listened to the rain on the roof until things were quiet again. Nobody ever came looking for me there, and I think they always knew exactly where I was.

entries.question: Who else lived in that home? Pick one person and tell me about an ordinary day with them.
entries.answer: It was Mama, Papa, my little brother Nico and me, and I will pick Mama, because her days all had the same shape. She was up before everyone and back from the market with her basket before we were awake. Then came the washing, and all afternoon she ironed other people's shirts by the kitchen window, where the light was best. She sang along with the radio, but only when she thought nobody was listening, so I learned to sit very still in the next room. At supper she never sat down; she ate standing at the stove and called it resting.

At supper Mama never sat down. She ate standing at the stove and called it resting.

entries.question: Tell me about a meal you remember from that home: who cooked, and who sat where.
entries.answer: Sunday lunch was the one meal we all sat down for. Mama cooked chicken stew with potatoes, and I was sent to the bakery on the corner for bread that was still warm when I got home. Papa sat at the head of the table, I sat on his left, and Nico sat across from me and kicked my shins under the oilcloth. Papa made grace extra long on purpose, because he knew how hungry we were, and gave thanks for the chicken, the potatoes, the bakery and every one of the neighbours. Mama would say his name once from the stove, and he would laugh and say amen.

entries.question: Was there a place outside that home that felt like yours, like a tree, a step, or a corner of the street?
entries.answer: The steps of the bakery on the corner. There were three stone steps, worn smooth in the middle, and the bottom one was mine. In the afternoons I sat there with my chin on my knees and watched the street: the ice cart, the big girls coming home from the high school, the dogs who knew which doors to wait at. The baker's wife, Belen, never once told me to move along. Near closing she would come out wiping her hands on her apron and put a broken roll in my lap without a word.

entries.question: What object from that home do you wish you still had?
entries.answer: The biscuit tin from under the stairs. We moved the year I turned twelve, somebody packed that space in a hurry, and the tin went into a box and the box went somewhere. I did not mind so much about the marbles or the ribbon. It was the photograph of my grandmother, Mama's mother, whom I never met, and it was the only picture of her I ever had. For years I looked inside every box Mama opened, and sometimes I still catch myself looking.

entries.question: Tell me about a night in that home you have never forgotten.
entries.answer: The night of the big storm, the year I was nine. The power went out with a bang somewhere down the street, and Papa found the kerosene in the dark by feel and lit the lamp. Mama pulled all the mattresses into the living room, and the four of us lay in a row listening to the rain hammer on the roof. Papa told us stories about when he was a boy, about a river and a borrowed bicycle, stories I had never heard before. I fell asleep before the last one ended, with the lamp still burning.

Papa told stories about when he was a boy. There was a river in them, and a borrowed bicycle. Rosa had never heard any of them before.

She fell asleep before the last one ended, with the lamp still burning.

entries.question: What is your earliest memory of your mother, or of the person who mothered you?
entries.answer: I was very small, maybe three, sitting on the kitchen floor while Mama ironed. She let me hold the end of a warm pillowcase and fold it, and of course I folded it all wrong. She did not fix it in front of me; she put it on the pile as if it were perfect. Years later she admitted she ironed it again after I went to bed. I think that was the first time I understood that she was on my side.

entries.question: What did you call your father as a child? Tell me about the first time you remember him.
entries.answer: I called him Papa, and Papa Tonyo when I wanted something, because that was what his friends at the shop called him. The first time I remember him clearly, he was carrying me on his shoulders to see the town fiesta parade, and I was holding on to his ears. He smelled of soap and bicycle oil. Every time the crowd cheered he gave a little jump so I would bounce, and I laughed so hard I forgot to watch the parade at all.

entries.question: What did your parents do for a living, and what did you understand about it as a child?
entries.answer: Papa repaired bicycles in a little shop two streets over, and Mama took in washing and ironing, and sewing at night on an old black machine with a foot pedal. I thought Papa could fix anything with wheels. I thought Mama's machine was a kind of animal, because it hummed and clattered and she talked to it when it jammed. I did not understand that the sewing paid for our school shoes until I was much older; I only knew that when the machine ran late into the night, something new was coming.

entries.question: Tell me about a time a parent surprised you, for better or for worse.
entries.answer: When I was fifteen I failed my mathematics exam and hid the report card under my mattress for a week. Papa found it, and I was sure he would shout, because he was strict about school. Instead he sat on the edge of my bed and told me he had failed the same exam twice. Then he spent every evening that month at the kitchen table with me, working through the problems with a pencil stub from the shop. I passed the next time, and he told all his customers as if I had won a prize.

Instead he sat on the edge of her bed and told her he had failed the same exam twice.

Then he spent every evening that month at the kitchen table with her, working through the problems with a pencil stub from the shop.

She passed the next time. Papa told all his customers as if she had won a prize.

entries.question: What is a sentence one of your parents used to say that you can still hear?
entries.answer: Mama used to say, 'Eat first, then cry.' She said it whenever one of us came home upset, and she meant it, because she put a plate in front of you before she asked a single question. As a girl I thought it was a strange thing to say, almost unkind. Now I say it to my own grandchildren, and I understand she was giving us time to be ready to talk.
entries.page:

When Rosa was small, she thought it was a strange thing to say, almost unkind.

Now she says it to her own grandchildren. She understands that Mama was giving them time to be ready to talk.

entries.question: Tell me about a grandparent, or the oldest person in your family you remember.
entries.answer: The oldest person I remember is Papa's aunt Carmen, who lived on her own at the end of our street. She wore black every day and kept peppermints in her apron pocket, one for each child who visited, never two. She could not read, but she knew the birthday of everyone in the family and reminded Papa a week ahead, so he had no excuse. Every year on my birthday she gave me a peppermint and a coin wrapped in a twist of newspaper, right up until I was a grown woman with children of my own.
entries.page:

Carmen could not read, but she knew the birthday of everyone in the family. A week ahead, she reminded Papa, so he had no excuse.

Every year on Rosa's birthday, Carmen gave her a peppermint and a coin wrapped in a twist of newspaper. She did it right up until Rosa was a grown woman with children of her own.

entries.question: Who in your family made you laugh the most? Tell me one story about them.
entries.answer: Nico, without a doubt. When he was about seven he decided to sell lemonade to the men coming out of Papa's shop, but we had no lemons, so he made it with vinegar and sugar. He charged one coin a cup and told everyone it was a special recipe from the city. Papa drank a whole cup in front of his customers without making a face, then paid Nico double to close the stand. To this day, when something goes wrong in a kitchen, someone in our family says it must be a special recipe from the city.
entries.page:

entries.question: Was there a family story everyone retold? Tell it the way it was always told.
entries.answer: The story of how Papa met Mama, and it was always Papa who told it. He said a girl brought a bicycle into the shop with a flat tyre, and he fixed it so slowly that she had to come back three days in a row. On the third day she told him she knew perfectly well it was only a flat tyre. Papa always finished the same way: 'And she has been checking my work ever since.' Mama rolled her eyes every single time, but she never once said it was not true.

entries.question: What did your family do on holidays or special days?
entries.answer: New Year's Eve was the big night on our street. Mama made a pot of sweet sticky rice with coconut that we ate at midnight, and Papa hung a lantern over the front door that he made himself from old bicycle spokes and coloured paper. When the church bells started, Nico and I were allowed to bang pots on the front step as loud as we liked. Afterwards everyone went from door to door wishing each other luck, and Belen from the bakery always gave us the first bread of the year.

Afterwards everyone on the street went from door to door wishing each other luck. Belen from the bakery always gave them the first bread of the year.

entries.question: Describe a place you went recently as if I were standing next to you.
entries.answer: Last month my daughter Lina drove me back to the old street for the first time in years. The house with the green door is painted blue now, and there is a gate where the front step used to be, but the bakery is still on the corner. The three steps are the same, worn smooth in the middle, and I sat on the bottom one while Lina went in for bread. A young woman came out from behind the counter to ask if I was all right, and I told her I used to live here. She gave me a roll from the morning batch, and I did not tell her why I laughed.

entries.question: What is a choice in front of you right now, and what is pulling you each way?
entries.answer: I still have Mama's old sewing machine, and my granddaughter Ana has asked if she can take it to her flat in the city. Part of me wants to say yes straight away, because a machine like that should be used, not dusted. But it is the last thing in my house that still sounds like Mama, and I am not sure I am ready to see that corner empty. I think I will give it to her, and ask her to sew me something on it first.

entries.question: Tell me about a small kindness this week, given or received.
entries.answer: My neighbour Teodoro is eighty-two and his eyes are getting worse, so on Tuesday I went over to read him his letters. One was from his son, who works overseas, with a photograph of a new grandson. He asked me to read it twice, and then a third time, slowly. When I left he gave me a bag of tomatoes from his garden and said we were even, but I think I got the better part of the deal.

When she got up to leave, he gave her a bag of tomatoes from his garden. He said they were even.

chapters.title: Rain on the Roof
chapters.text:
The front door was green, and it stuck every time it rained. It took a shoulder and a push before it gave.

Inside, the house smelled of rice cooking and floor wax, and a little of the kerosene Papa kept by the lamp for when the power went out. Mama always had the radio on low in the kitchen, so there was music before there was anybody talking.

Even now, the smell of floor wax makes Rosa want to take her shoes off at the door.

Under the stairs was where the brooms were kept. At the back there was a gap just big enough for Rosa.

She kept a biscuit tin there, with a blue ribbon tied around it. Inside were two marbles, one cloudy and one clear, and the only photograph she had of her grandmother, in a dress with a white collar.

When the house got loud, Rosa crawled in with the tin on her knees and listened to the rain on the roof until things were quiet again.

Nobody ever came looking for her there. She thinks they always knew exactly where she was.

* * *

Four people lived in that house: Mama, Papa, Rosa's little brother Nico, and Rosa. Mama's days all had the same shape.

She was up before everyone, and back from the market with her basket before the children were awake. Then came the washing. All afternoon she ironed other people's shirts by the kitchen window, where the light was best.

The radio stayed on low. Mama sang along with it, but only when she thought nobody was listening, so Rosa learned to sit very still in the next room.

At supper Mama never sat down. She ate standing at the stove and called it resting.

* * *

Sunday lunch was the one meal they all sat down for.

Mama cooked chicken stew with potatoes, and Rosa was sent to the bakery on the corner for bread. It was still warm when she got home.

Papa sat at the head of the table, with Rosa on his left. Nico sat across from her and kicked her shins under the oilcloth.

Papa made grace extra long on purpose, because he knew how hungry they were. He gave thanks for the chicken, for the potatoes, for the bakery, and for every one of the neighbours.

Mama would say his name once from the stove.

Papa would laugh and say amen.

* * *

The bakery on the corner had three stone steps, worn smooth in the middle. The bottom one was Rosa's.

In the afternoons she sat there with her chin on her knees and watched the street: the ice cart, the big girls coming home from the high school, the dogs who knew which doors to wait at.

The baker's wife, Belen, never once told her to move along. Near closing, Belen would come out wiping her hands on her apron and put a broken roll in Rosa's lap without a word.

* * *

The year Rosa was nine, there was a big storm. The power went out with a bang somewhere down the street.

Papa found the kerosene in the dark by feel, the kerosene he kept by the lamp for when the power went out, and lit the lamp.

Mama pulled all the mattresses into the living room, and the four of them lay in a row listening to the rain hammer on the roof.

Papa told them stories from when he was a boy, about a river and a borrowed bicycle. Rosa had never heard them before.

She fell asleep before the last one ended, with the lamp still burning.

* * *

They moved the year Rosa turned twelve. Somebody packed the space under the stairs in a hurry, and the biscuit tin went into a box, and the box went somewhere.

She did not mind so much about the marbles, or the ribbon. It was the photograph she minded. Her grandmother was Mama's mother, and Rosa never met her. The woman in the dress with the white collar was the only picture of her Rosa ever had.

For years Rosa looked inside every box Mama opened.

Sometimes she still catches herself looking.
threads: Rain seems to run through this house: it made the green door stick, it was what you listened to under the stairs until things were quiet, and it hammered on the roof the night of the storm while Papa told his stories.

You seem often to have been the one listening or watching: sitting very still while Mama sang, listening from under the stairs, watching the street from the bottom bakery step, hearing Papa's stories for the first time.

It is possible that some of the care in these stories came without words: nobody came looking for you under the stairs though you think they knew where you were, and Belen put a broken roll in your lap without saying anything.

people.name: Papa
people.note: Kept kerosene by the lamp for when the power went out. Sat at the head of the table on Sundays. Made grace extra long on purpose because he knew how hungry the children were. Thanked the chicken, potatoes, bakery and every neighbour. Laughed and said amen when Mama said his name. Called Papa Tonyo by his friends at the shop; Rosa used 'Papa Tonyo' when she wanted something. Smelled of soap and bicycle oil. Carried Rosa on his shoulders at the town fiesta parade and jumped when the crowd cheered so she would bounce. Repaired bicycles in a little shop two streets over. Rosa thought he could fix anything with wheels. Strict about school. When Rosa failed maths at fifteen, he told her he had failed the same exam twice and studied with her every evening that month with a pencil stub from the shop. Told all his customers when she passed. Always the one to tell the story of how he met Mama; ended it with 'And she has been checking my work ever since.'

people.name: Mama
people.note: Kept the radio on low in the kitchen. Cooked chicken stew with potatoes for Sunday lunch. Said Papa's name once from the stove during grace. When Rosa was about three, let her fold a warm pillowcase while ironing, put it on the pile as if perfect, and years later admitted she re-ironed it after Rosa went to bed. Took in washing and ironing, and sewed at night on an old black foot-pedal machine. She talked to it when it jammed. Came to Papa's shop with a flat tyre on her bicycle, returned three days in a row, and on the third day said she knew it was only a flat tyre. Rolled her eyes every time the story was told but never said it was untrue.

people.name: Rosa's grandmother
people.note: Rosa's only photograph of her shows her in a dress with a white collar, kept in the biscuit tin. Rosa never met her. The photograph in the biscuit tin was the only picture of her Rosa ever had.

people.name: Nico
people.note: Lived in the childhood home with Rosa, Mama and Papa. Sat across from Rosa at Sunday lunch and kicked her shins under the oilcloth. The family member who made Rosa laugh the most. At about seven he sold vinegar-and-sugar lemonade outside Papa's shop for one coin a cup, calling it a special recipe from the city.

people.name: Belen
people.note: Never told Rosa to move along from the bakery steps. Near closing she came out wiping her hands on her apron and put a broken roll in Rosa's lap without a word. On New Year's Eve she always gave Rosa and Nico the first bread of the year.

people.name: Rosa's grandchildren
people.note: Rosa says 'Eat first, then cry' to them now.

people.name: Carmen
people.note: Oldest person Rosa remembers. Lived alone at the end of the street, wore black every day, kept peppermints in her apron pocket, one for each child who visited, never two. Could not read but knew everyone's birthday and reminded Papa a week ahead. Gave Rosa a peppermint and a coin in a twist of newspaper every birthday, until Rosa was a grown woman with children.

people.name: Ana
people.note: Has asked to take Mama's old sewing machine to her flat in the city.

people.name: Teodoro
people.note: Eighty-two, eyesight failing. Rosa reads him his letters. His son works overseas and sent a letter with a photograph of a new grandson. Gave Rosa a bag of garden tomatoes.

Rosa minded the loss of the photograph more than the marbles or the ribbon.
For years Rosa looked inside every box Mama opened; she sometimes still catches herself looking.
The year Rosa was nine, a big storm knocked out the power with a bang somewhere down the street.
Papa found the kerosene in the dark by feel and lit the lamp.
Mama pulled all the mattresses into the living room and the four of them lay in a row listening to the rain on the roof.
Papa told stories from his boyhood about a river and a borrowed bicycle, which Rosa had never heard before.
Rosa fell asleep before the last story ended, with the lamp still burning.
Rosa's earliest memory of Mama is at about age three, folding a warm pillowcase on the kitchen floor.
Rosa thinks that was the first time she understood Mama was on her side.
Rosa called her father Papa, and Papa Tonyo when she wanted something.
Rosa's first clear memory of Papa is being carried on his shoulders at the town fiesta parade.
Rosa thought Mama's sewing machine was a kind of animal because it hummed and clattered.
When the machine ran late into the night, Rosa knew something new was coming.
Rosa learned much later that the sewing paid for the school shoes.
At fifteen Rosa failed her mathematics exam and hid the report card under her mattress for a week.
Papa found it, sat on the edge of her bed and said he had failed the same exam twice.
Rosa passed the exam the next time.
Papa told all his customers about it as if she had won a prize.
Mama's saying was 'Eat first, then cry.' She said it whenever one of the children came home upset.
Mama put a plate in front of you before she asked a single question.
As a child Rosa thought the saying strange, almost unkind.
Rosa now says it to her own grandchildren and understands Mama was giving them time to be ready to talk.
Carmen could not read but knew the birthday of everyone in the family.
Carmen gave Rosa a peppermint and a coin wrapped in newspaper every birthday into Rosa's adulthood.
Papa drank a whole cup of Nico's vinegar lemonade in front of his customers without making a face, then paid Nico double to close the stand.
In Rosa's family, when something goes wrong in a kitchen, someone says it must be a special recipe from the city.
The family story everyone retold was how Papa met Mama, always told by Papa.
Papa fixed Mama's flat tyre so slowly that she had to come back three days in a row.
On the third day Mama told him she knew perfectly well it was only a flat tyre.
Papa always ended the story: 'And she has been checking my work ever since.'
Mama rolled her eyes every time but never once said it was not true.
New Year's Eve was the big night on Rosa's street.
Mama made sweet sticky rice with coconut, eaten at midnight on New Year's Eve.
Papa made a lantern from old bicycle spokes and coloured paper and hung it over the front door on New Year's Eve.
When the church bells started, Rosa and Nico could bang pots on the front step as loud as they liked.
After midnight everyone went door to door wishing each other luck.
Last month Rosa sat on the bottom bakery step while Lina bought bread.
A young woman from the bakery asked if Rosa was all right and gave her a roll from the morning batch.
Rosa laughed and did not tell the young woman why.
Rosa still has Mama's old sewing machine.
It is the last thing in Rosa's house that still sounds like Mama.
Rosa thinks she will give it to Ana and ask her to sew something for Rosa on it first.
On Tuesday this week Rosa went to Teodoro's to read him his letters.
Teodoro asked Rosa to read his son's letter twice, then a third time, slowly.
Teodoro said he and Rosa were even; Rosa thinks she got the better part of the deal.
